newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: E.Asian Grains - Korea seen buying Canadian wheat.
newsitem.headline: E.Asian Grains - Korea seen buying Canadian wheat.

text.p: South Korean feed processors are expected to buy more than 200,000 tonnes of Canadian feed wheat by December to cover their needs for February/March shipment, traders said on Monday.
Feed wheat prices currently appear more attractive than corn prices, they said.

"Local buyers are expected to buy more than two 50,000-tonne cargoes of Canadian feed wheat for February and (the same amount for) March shipment by December," said a grain trader with the National Livestock Cooperatives Federation (NLCF).
"Feed wheat prices have recently been traded at about $10 below corn prices," said a trader with Cheiljedang Corp.

South Korean buyers will probably hold back their corn purchases until after the U.S. Department of Agriculture's (USDA) crop production and world agricutural supply and demand report is released on Tuesday, traders said.

"Most traders seem to believe there will be an increase in the U.S. corn crop for November from that for October. If it is more than the market expectation of 9.2-9.3 billion bushels, corn price will show another drop," the trader in Cheiljedang Corp said.
"If it is within the market expectation, corn prices will move sideways," the trader added.

"For corn, most local buyers are expected to remain on the sidelines for the time being regardless of the USDA report as they have already covered their corn needs by March shipment and some have covered for mid-1997 shipments," the NLCF trader said.
The NLCF trader said the recent strong freight premium also shoved buyers away from the market.

"The freight premium to South Korean ports from the Pacific Northwest remains unchanged at US$14 per tonne," the trader said. He added that the freight premium from the U.S. Gulf also remained unchanged at $24 per tonne.

In Tokyo, Japanese buyers remain unfazed by the USDA report since traders have already bought the January/March shipment for U.S. corn, and are expected to wait for the right time to buy for April/June deliveries until the year-end.
"We've covered all corn requirement for the first quarter of next year," a corn trader of a major Japanese trade house said. "And it's too early to buy for the April/June period."
Traders said they basically expected a bearish USDA November crop production report Tuesday, but added smaller-than-estimated figures could spark fresh buying.
Most traders estimate the U.S. corn crop to be around 9.2-9.3 billion bushels against the USDA October report forecast of 9.012 billion bushels.

A concern for Japanese traders is the recent rise of the U.S. Gulf/Japan freight rate. Nearby freight rates on the U.S. Gulf/Japan grain route were quoted on Monday at up to $26 per tonne, against $24.50 last Thursday.
"The freight rate showed rapid gains last week because of Chinese buying. This will motivate some Japanese importers to buy this week," a trader said.

To diversify their feed sources, a corn mission by Japanese trade houses and feed makers has flown to Argentina for talks with farmers there. Corn is used for making feed in Japan. The 11-member mission is visiting Argentina November 5.

"Given our over-dependence on American corn, it makes great sense to buy more from Argentine," another corn trader said. "We'll get specific production figures of Argentine corn around next January, and will work out (our) import strategy then."

Japan depends heavily on U.S. corn because of a ban on Chinese corn exports since 1994. In the first nine months of this year, Japan bought 7,387,690 tonnes of corn and 98.9 percent of this came from the United States.

Japanese importers have covered U.S. soybean shipments for December shipment, and are gradually buying for first half of January with premiums at 135 U.S. cents a bushel over the Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) January futures contract.
In Taiwan, buyers will probably tender for 26,000 tonnes of corn and 38,000 tonnes of soybeans this week, traders said.
Philippine flour firms are expected to stay out of the market due to ample supplies, traders said.
